title: Putting It Together: Obstacle Avoidance From Scratch
description: Sequence, decision, loop — all three, in one program you design yourself, to build the exact behaviour ARIA's real ultrasonic sensor needs.

content.value: This is the behaviour Module 7's ultrasonic sensor was always building toward: a robot that drives forward, and the moment it senses a wall ahead, turns instead of crashing into it — then keeps going, forever, reacting to whatever it finds next.

Read that shape carefully: a loop (forever) containing a decision (if/else), which itself contains simple sequence steps. All three shapes from this module, nested inside each other. That's not a coincidence — real programs are built exactly this way, shapes nested inside shapes.

content.title: 🧩 Build obstacle avoidance
content.hint: Try to solve this with a single repeat forever containing one if/else — no other blocks needed outside it.

content.value: Why This Counts as a Milestone

Every previous maze in this module had one fixed correct path. This one is different: the same repeat-forever-with-if program you just wrote would work on a completely different maze layout too, because it isn't memorising a path — it's reacting to whatever wall it happens to find, one decision at a time. That's the real definition of an autonomous behaviour, and you just built one.
You've now finished every block-based lesson this course has. Next module takes this exact same program and rewrites it, line for line, as real Python — the bridge from blocks to code.

Key takeaway: nesting a decision inside a loop is how a program reacts continuously to a changing situation, rather than following one fixed memorised path. That's the shape behind every truly autonomous robot behaviour.

quiz.question: Why does a 'repeat forever containing an if/else' program count as more genuinely autonomous than a long hardcoded sequence that happens to solve the same maze?
options: It reacts to whatever wall it actually finds rather than memorising one fixed path, so it would still work on a different maze layout
There's no real difference between the two approaches
quiz.explain: A hardcoded sequence only works for the exact maze it was written for. A reactive if/else-in-a-loop program generalises to situations it's never seen.

quiz.question: In `repeat forever: if wall ahead: turn, else: move forward`, which shape from this module contains which?
options: A loop contains a decision, which contains sequence steps
None of the shapes are nested — they're all separate
quiz.explain: The outermost shape is the loop; inside it sits a decision; inside each branch of the decision sits a simple sequence step.
